title: DATA CLEANING REALM
tagline: Master the journey from raw data to a clean and understandable dataset
description: Embark on the foundational MBA Machine Learning journey. Venture into the Import Forge, brave the Missing Value Dungeon, harness the Category Forge, scale the Visualization Tower, and conquer the Clean Data Trial.

levels.title: Meet the Data
levels.description: Understand tabular datasets, explore DataFrame architecture, and master delimiters.

lessons.title: Tabular Datasets & DataFrames
lessons.content:
In data science and business analytics, data is primarily organized in tabular format.

• Rows represent individual records or observations (e.g., individual student performance entries).
• Columns represent variables or attributes (e.g., Student_ID, Name, Marks, Course).

In Python, the `pandas` library represents this table as a `DataFrame`.
lessons.codeExample:
import pandas as pd

# A DataFrame is a 2D labeled data structure with rows and columns
print("Pandas imported successfully")
lessons.outputExample: Pandas imported successfully
lessons.tip: Think of a DataFrame as an interactive, programmatic spreadsheet table inside Python.

lessons.title: Delimiters & File Formats
lessons.content:
Raw data files store rows as lines of text. A delimiter is the special character used to separate column values within each line.

• CSV (Comma-Separated Values): uses a comma (`,`) as the delimiter.
• TSV (Tab-Separated Values): uses a tab (`\t`).
• Other formats may use semicolons (`;`) or vertical pipes (`|`).
lessons.codeExample:
# Raw CSV line representation:
# 101,Aarav,M,20,Data Science,Delhi,5.5,92,78
print("Comma is the standard CSV separator")
lessons.outputExample: Comma is the standard CSV separator
lessons.tip: Always check your file's delimiter if columns appear bundled together as one long string.

lessons.title: Inspecting Data Dimensions
lessons.content:
Once imported, pandas provides quick methods to inspect the structure of your DataFrame:

• `df.shape`: returns `(rows, columns)` tuple.
• `df.columns`: lists all variable names.
• `df.head()`: previews the first 5 observations.
lessons.codeExample:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")
print("Shape:", df.shape)
print("Columns:", list(df.columns[:4]))
lessons.outputExample:
Shape: (10, 9)
Columns: ['Student_ID', 'Name', 'Gender', 'Age']
lessons.tip: Always inspect df.shape immediately after loading to confirm all rows and columns were imported.

levels.title: Data Import Forge
levels.description: Harness pd.read_csv(), open(), web URL streams, and pd.read_excel() to import external data.

lessons.title: Reading CSV with pandas
lessons.content:
The standard and most convenient method to import CSV data in Python is `pd.read_csv()`.

`pd.read_csv()` automatically parses headers, detects types, and loads records into a structured DataFrame ready for analytics.
lessons.codeExample:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")
print(df.head(2))
lessons.outputExample:
Student_ID   Name Gender  Age        Course   City  Study_Hours  Attendance  Marks
0         101  Aarav      M   20  Data Science  Delhi          5.5        92.0   78.0
1         102   Diya      F   21   ML           Mumbai         6.0        88.0    NaN
lessons.tip: pd.read_csv() handles file paths, parsing, and type conversions in a single invocation.

lessons.title: Python's Built-In open() Method
lessons.content:
Python includes a built-in `open()` function for working with raw files.

While `open()` allows reading lines of text into Python strings, it does not structure tabular data or parse columns into vectors. For analytical tasks, `pd.read_csv()` builds on top of low-level readers to create structured DataFrames.
lessons.codeExample:
# Low-level file opening in Python
with open("student_performance.csv", "r") as f:
    first_line = f.readline().strip()
print("Header line:", first_line)
lessons.outputExample: Header line: Student_ID,Name,Gender,Age,Course,City,Study_Hours,Attendance,Marks
lessons.tip: Use open() when reading arbitrary raw text files; use pd.read_csv() when you need tabular analysis.

lessons.title: Reading Data from a URL
lessons.content:
In cloud and collaborative workflows, datasets often reside online.

Instead of manually downloading files to your desktop, `pd.read_csv()` accepts web URLs directly (HTTP/HTTPS) and streams remote CSV data straight into your workspace!
lessons.codeExample:
# Reading from remote web sources directly:
# df_web = pd.read_csv("https://example.com/dataset.csv")
print("URL streams load directly into memory")
lessons.outputExample: URL streams load directly into memory
lessons.tip: Ensure the URL points to raw CSV text rather than an HTML download page.

lessons.title: Importing Excel Files (.xls / .xlsx)
lessons.content:
Excel spreadsheets often store business reports.

Pandas provides `pd.read_excel()` to load `.xls` and `.xlsx` workbooks. By default, it reads the first worksheet, or you can specify `sheet_name='Sheet1'`.
lessons.codeExample:
import pandas as pd

# Reading an Excel workbook:
# df_excel = pd.read_excel("student_performance.xlsx", sheet_name="Students")
print("pd.read_excel handles .xlsx spreadsheets")
lessons.outputExample: pd.read_excel handles .xlsx spreadsheets
lessons.tip: Reading modern .xlsx files relies on engines like openpyxl behind the scenes.

levels.title: Data Export Workshop
levels.description: Master df.to_csv(), df.to_excel(), index=False, ExcelWriter for multiple sheets, and raw data preservation.

lessons.title: Writing to CSV & index=False
lessons.content:
To save a DataFrame back to disk, pandas provides `df.to_csv("filename.csv")`.

Crucial Academic Concept: By default, pandas writes its integer index (0, 1, 2...) into the file. Using `index=False` prevents pandas from adding the row index as an unwanted extra column in your output file!
lessons.codeExample:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")

# Save without row index numbers:
df.to_csv("cleaned.csv", index=False)
print("Saved raw data to 'cleaned.csv' with index=False")
lessons.outputExample: Saved raw data to 'cleaned.csv' with index=False
lessons.tip: Always specify index=False unless your index has meaningful labels (such as dates).

lessons.title: Writing to Excel (.xlsx)
lessons.content:
To generate an Excel spreadsheet for business stakeholders, use `df.to_excel("cleaned.xlsx", index=False)`.

Like `to_csv()`, passing `index=False` ensures clean spreadsheet columns without redundant index numbers.
lessons.codeExample:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")

# Export to an Excel workbook
df.to_excel("cleaned.xlsx", index=False)
print("Saved data to 'cleaned.xlsx'")
lessons.outputExample: Saved data to 'cleaned.xlsx'
lessons.tip: Excel files make it easy for non-technical team members to inspect results.

lessons.title: Multiple Worksheets with ExcelWriter
lessons.content:
Often you need to output multiple related tables into a single workbook.

`pd.ExcelWriter()` with a Python context manager (`with`) allows writing multiple DataFrames to distinct worksheets (e.g. 'Students' and 'Sales') within one file!
lessons.codeExample:
import pandas as pd
students = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")
sales = pd.read_csv("sales_data.csv")

# Create multi-sheet workbook using openpyxl engine:
with pd.ExcelWriter("final_report.xlsx", engine="openpyxl") as writer:
    students.to_excel(writer, sheet_name="Students", index=False)
    sales.to_excel(writer, sheet_name="Sales", index=False)
print("Saved multi-sheet workbook")
lessons.outputExample: Saved multi-sheet workbook
lessons.tip: ExcelWriter automatically saves and closes the file when exiting the with-block.

lessons.title: Golden Rule: Raw Data Preservation
lessons.content:
Fundamental Teaching Principle from the Classroom Notes:

Always preserve the original/raw dataset! Never perform destructive in-place modifications that overwrite your raw source files.

Always perform cleaning on a working copy and save the cleaned result under a distinct filename (e.g., `cleaned_student_performance.csv`).
lessons.codeExample:
# Golden Rule: Keep raw source intact
# df_raw = pd.read_csv("raw_data.csv")
# df_clean = df_raw.copy()
# df_clean.to_csv("cleaned_data.csv", index=False)
print("Preserve raw data -> Output to separate cleaned file")
lessons.outputExample: Preserve raw data -> Output to separate cleaned file
lessons.tip: If a cleaning step is flawed, you can always reload the pristine raw dataset.

challenges.title: Purpose of index=False
challenges.instructions: What is the primary purpose of specifying index=False when exporting with to_csv() or to_excel()?
challenges.question: Why do we pass index=False?
options: A. Prevents the DataFrame's row index from being written as an unnecessary extra column
B. Deletes all row indices from computer RAM permanently
C. Sorts the output file in reverse order
D. Hides the column headers in the spreadsheet
challenges.answer: A. Prevents the DataFrame's row index from being written as an unnecessary extra column
hints: Think about what pandas row numbers (0, 1, 2...) would do if saved into the CSV.
challenges.explanation: Correct! index=False prevents pandas from writing its integer index into the file as an extra unneeded column.

challenges.title: Raw Data Preservation
challenges.instructions: According to best analytical practices emphasized in the course notes, how should cleaned data be saved?
challenges.question: What is the golden rule for saving cleaned datasets?
options: A. Save cleaned data under a separate filename to preserve the raw dataset intact
B. Overwrite the original raw file immediately without backup
C. Delete the original file from the server
D. Never save cleaned data to disk
challenges.answer: A. Save cleaned data under a separate filename to preserve the raw dataset intact
hints: Raw data should always be preserved so analyses can be reproduced or audited.
challenges.explanation: Spot on! Always preserve the original raw dataset and save cleaned outputs to separate files.

levels.title: Missing Value Dungeon
levels.description: Detect missingness with isna().sum(), calculate percentages, drop rows with dropna(), impute with median, and execute ffill/bfill.

lessons.title: Detecting Missing Values (isna & sum)
lessons.content:
Real-world datasets frequently contain missing values (represented as `NaN` — Not a Number in pandas).

• `df.isna()`: returns `True` for missing cells and `False` for valid observations.
• `df.isna().sum()`: sums the `True` values across each column, yielding the exact missing value count per attribute.
lessons.codeExample:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")

# Count missing values per column:
print(df.isna().sum())
lessons.outputExample:
Student_ID     0
Name           0
Gender         1
Age            0
Course         0
City           2
Study_Hours    0
Attendance     2
Marks          2
dtype: int64
lessons.tip: Both isna() and isnull() are aliases in pandas and produce identical results.

lessons.title: Calculating Missing Percentages
lessons.content:
To understand the severity of missingness relative to sample size, compute the percentage of missing values per column:

`df.isna().mean() * 100`

Because Python evaluates `True` as `1` and `False` as `0`, the mean of a boolean column gives the proportion of missing values. Multiplying by 100 gives the percentage.
lessons.codeExample:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")

# Percentage of missing observations per variable:
print(df.isna().mean() * 100)
lessons.outputExample:
Student_ID      0.0
Name            0.0
Gender         10.0
Age             0.0
Course          0.0
City           20.0
Study_Hours     0.0
Attendance     20.0
Marks          20.0
dtype: float64
lessons.tip: A column with 80% missing data may need to be dropped, while 5% missing can be imputed.

lessons.title: Removing Missing Values (dropna)
lessons.content:
When missing rows cannot be reliably filled, `df.dropna()` removes incomplete observations.

To avoid indiscriminately deleting rows across all columns, specify the `subset` argument:

`df_dropped = df.dropna(subset=["Marks"])`

Academic Note: Dropping rows reduces your sample size. This decision should always be justified and documented.
lessons.codeExample:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")

df_dropped = df.dropna(subset=["Marks"])
print(f"Original rows: {len(df)}, After dropping missing Marks: {len(df_dropped)}")
lessons.outputExample: Original rows: 10, After dropping missing Marks: 8
lessons.tip: Always inspect length before and after dropna() to monitor lost sample size.

lessons.title: Filling Missing Values with Median
lessons.content:
Rather than discarding valuable observations, we can impute missing numeric entries with a summary statistic.

`df["Marks"] = df["Marks"].fillna(df["Marks"].median())`

Why Median? The median represents the middle score and is robust to extreme outliers or skewed distributions.
lessons.codeExample:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")

median_marks = df["Marks"].median()
print("Median Marks:", median_marks)

df["Marks"] = df["Marks"].fillna(median_marks)
print("Remaining missing Marks:", df["Marks"].isna().sum())
lessons.outputExample:
Median Marks: 74.0
Remaining missing Marks: 0
lessons.tip: For skewed data, median is often preferred over mean to avoid outlier distortion.

lessons.title: Forward Fill (ffill) & Backward Fill (bfill)
lessons.content:
In ordered or time-series data, sequential proximity has substantive meaning.

• `ffill()` (Forward Fill): carries the previous available observation forward into subsequent missing cells.
• `bfill()` (Backward Fill): carries the next available observation backward into preceding missing cells.
lessons.codeExample:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")

# Carry previous attendance observation forward:
df["Attendance"] = df["Attendance"].ffill()
print("Attendance missing after ffill:", df["Attendance"].isna().sum())
lessons.outputExample: Attendance missing after ffill: 0
lessons.tip: Forward fill is especially meaningful when data arrives chronologically.

challenges.title: Missing Value Percentage

challenges.question: How does df.isna().mean() * 100 work mathematically?
options: A. True is treated as 1 and False as 0, so the mean gives the proportion of missing values
B. It multiplies row counts by 100 automatically
C. mean() calculates the median of non-missing rows
D. It divides the column standard deviation by sample size
challenges.answer: A. True is treated as 1 and False as 0, so the mean gives the proportion of missing values
hints: In Python, boolean True == 1 and False == 0.
challenges.explanation: Correct! True evaluates as 1 and False as 0, so the mean represents the proportion; multiplying by 100 converts it to a percentage.

challenges.starterCode:

hints: Use .ffill() to carry the previous available value forward.
challenges.explanation: Brilliant! You executed forward fill to impute missing attendance values.

levels.title: Category Forge
levels.description: Convert categorical columns to numerical indicators with pd.get_dummies(), handle missing categories, and avoid the dummy-variable trap.

lessons.title: Categorical Data & Pre-Encoding
lessons.content:
Statistical and machine-learning models require numerical input. Categorical variables (such as Gender or Course) must be encoded as numbers.

Crucial Teaching Step from Notes: If a categorical column contains missing values, replace them with an explicit category (e.g., `'Unknown'`) before encoding:

`df["Gender"] = df["Gender"].fillna("Unknown")`

This ensures missing observations are not silently lost during dummy variable generation.
lessons.codeExample:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")

# Explicitly handle missing categorical entries:
df["Gender"] = df["Gender"].fillna("Unknown")
print(df["Gender"].value_counts())
lessons.outputExample:
Gender
M          5
F          4
Unknown    1
Name: count, dtype: int64
lessons.tip: Handling missing categories explicitly preserves row counts and prevents silent omissions.

lessons.title: Creating Dummy Variables (get_dummies)
lessons.content:
Pandas creates binary (0/1) indicator columns using `pd.get_dummies()`.

Each unique category receives its own indicator column. Passing `dtype=int` ensures indicators are stored as clean 0 and 1 integers instead of boolean True/False.
lessons.codeExample:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")
df["Gender"] = df["Gender"].fillna("Unknown")

# Generate dummy indicator columns:
df_dummies = pd.get_dummies(df, columns=["Gender"], dtype=int)
print([c for c in df_dummies.columns if "Gender" in c])
lessons.outputExample: ['Gender_F', 'Gender_M', 'Gender_Unknown']
lessons.tip: Dummy columns let models measure category-specific intercept effects.

lessons.title: The Dummy-Variable Trap & drop_first=True
lessons.content:
The Dummy-Variable Trap occurs when all category columns are included alongside an intercept term in a regression model.

Because the sum of all dummy indicators equals 1 for every observation, the columns suffer from perfect linear dependence (perfect multicollinearity)!

Solution: Use `drop_first=True`. Dropping one category removes linear dependence and establishes the omitted category as the reference/baseline group.
lessons.codeExample:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")

# Avoid multicollinearity with drop_first=True:
df_course = pd.get_dummies(df, columns=["Course"], drop_first=True, dtype=int)
print([c for c in df_course.columns if "Course" in c])
lessons.outputExample: ['Course_Data Science', 'Course_Machine Learning']
lessons.tip: Business Analytics was dropped and acts as the reference baseline group against which others are compared.

challenges.title: The Dummy-Variable Trap
challenges.instructions: What problem does drop_first=True prevent when creating dummy variables?
challenges.question: What is the purpose of drop_first=True in dummy encoding?
options: A. Perfect linear dependence (multicollinearity) when an intercept is included
B. Accidental deletion of numerical columns
C. Formatting numbers as strings
D. Exceeding memory limits
challenges.answer: A. Perfect linear dependence (multicollinearity) when an intercept is included
hints: If all k category indicators sum to 1, they are perfectly collinear with the model intercept.
challenges.explanation: Correct! If all k dummy columns are included with an intercept, they are perfectly linearly dependent. drop_first=True resolves this.

challenges.title: Reference Group Role
challenges.instructions: When drop_first=True omits the first category column, what role does that omitted category serve in statistical models?
challenges.question: What happens to the omitted category?
options: A. It serves as the baseline / reference group against which other categories are compared
B. It is permanently deleted from the raw file
C. It is converted into NaN
D. It is assigned a value of infinity
challenges.answer: A. It serves as the baseline / reference group against which other categories are compared
hints: The model intercept captures the expected value of the baseline/reference group.
challenges.explanation: Exact! The omitted category serves as the benchmark reference group.

challenges.title: Encode Course with drop_first=True
challenges.instructions: Complete the pd.get_dummies call to encode the 'Course' column using drop_first=True and dtype=int.
challenges.starterCode:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")
df_encoded = pd.get_dummies(df, columns=["Course"], ________=True, dtype=int)
print([c for c in df_encoded.columns if "Course" in c])
challenges.solution:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")
df_encoded = pd.get_dummies(df, columns=["Course"], drop_first=True, dtype=int)
print([c for c in df_encoded.columns if "Course" in c])
hints: Specify drop_first=True as the argument.
challenges.explanation: Well done! You generated dummy variables and avoided the dummy-variable trap.

levels.title: Visualization Tower
levels.description: Ascend the tower with matplotlib scatter plots, histograms with bins=8, boxplots, and categorical boxplots.

lessons.title: Scatter Plots: Association vs Causation
lessons.content:
Scatter plots display the relationship between two continuous numeric variables.

`plt.scatter(df["Study_Hours"], df["Marks"])`

Academic Distinction from Notes: A scatter plot helps identify associations, clusters, and potential outliers. However, an observed association between variables does NOT by itself prove causation!
lessons.codeExample:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")

plt.scatter(df["Study_Hours"], df["Marks"])
plt.xlabel("Study hours")
plt.ylabel("Marks")
plt.title("Study Hours vs Marks")
plt.show()
lessons.outputExample: Scatter plot displayed: positive association between Study Hours & Marks
lessons.tip: Always label your axes with plt.xlabel() and plt.ylabel() so viewers understand the units.

chartPreview.title: Study Hours vs Marks (Scatter Plot)
chartPreview.subtitle: Positive association visible between study investment and student exam scores.

lessons.title: Histograms: Frequency Distributions
lessons.content:
A histogram displays the frequency distribution of a single numeric variable.

`plt.hist(df["Marks"].dropna(), bins=8)`

• `dropna()` removes missing entries before plotting.
• `bins=8` divides the numeric score range into 8 equal intervals. The y-axis shows the count of observations falling within each interval.
lessons.codeExample:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")

plt.hist(df["Marks"].dropna(), bins=8)
plt.xlabel("Marks")
plt.ylabel("Frequency")
plt.title("Distribution of Marks")
plt.show()
lessons.outputExample: Histogram displayed: Marks divided into 8 frequency bins
lessons.tip: The choice of bins affects the visual shape of the distribution.

lessons.title: Boxplots: Five-Number Summary
lessons.content:
A boxplot summarizes the distribution of a numeric variable using five key statistics:

1. Minimum (lower whisker)
2. First Quartile (Q1 - 25th percentile)
3. Median (middle line - 50th percentile)
4. Third Quartile (Q3 - 75th percentile)
5. Maximum (upper whisker)

Points plotted beyond the whiskers indicate potential outliers.
lessons.codeExample:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")

plt.boxplot(df["Marks"].dropna())
plt.ylabel("Marks")
plt.title("Boxplot of Marks")
plt.show()
lessons.outputExample: Boxplot displayed: Median at 74.0, Q1 at 66.5, Q3 at 86.5
lessons.tip: The central box represents the Interquartile Range (IQR), containing the middle 50% of data.

chartPreview.title: Boxplot of Marks
chartPreview.subtitle: Five-number summary showing median, quartiles, and range.

lessons.title: Boxplots by Category
lessons.content:
To compare distributions across different groups, pandas provides grouped boxplots:

`df.boxplot(column="Marks", by="Course")`

This generates side-by-side boxplots for each course category, allowing immediate visual comparison of group medians, spread, and outliers.
lessons.codeExample:
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")

df.boxplot(column="Marks", by="Course")
plt.suptitle("")
plt.title("Marks by Course")
plt.ylabel("Marks")
plt.show()

challenges.title: Scatter Plot & Causation
challenges.instructions: When analyzing a positive pattern in a scatter plot between Study Hours and Marks, what critical distinction must be observed?
challenges.question: What does a scatter plot demonstrate?
options: A. It displays statistical association between two numeric variables, but association does not prove causation
B. It proves that studying directly causes high marks in 100% of scenarios
C. It calculates the percentage of missing values
D. It generates multiple Excel sheets
challenges.answer: A. It displays statistical association between two numeric variables, but association does not prove causation
hints: Remember the core statistical maxim: correlation/association does not imply causation.
challenges.explanation: Correct! A scatter plot reveals empirical association, but confounding variables or reverse causality mean association does not prove causation.

challenges.title: Metrics Summarized by a Boxplot
challenges.instructions: Which set of statistical metrics is directly visualized by a boxplot?
challenges.question: What metrics does a boxplot display?
options: A. Median, quartiles, interquartile range (IQR), whiskers, and potential outliers
B. P-values and regression coefficients only
C. Standard error of the mean only
D. Cumulative probability distribution functions
challenges.answer: A. Median, quartiles, interquartile range (IQR), whiskers, and potential outliers
hints: A boxplot provides a five-number summary.
challenges.explanation: Correct! Boxplots summarize the median, quartiles (Q1, Q3), interquartile range, whiskers, and outlying points.

levels.title: The Clean Data Trial
levels.description: Execute the full classroom data-cleaning workflow: READ -> INSPECT -> IMPUTE -> ENCODE -> VISUALIZE -> EXPORT.

lessons.title: The Grand Data-Cleaning Trial
lessons.content:
Welcome to the culmination of Module 1: The Clean Data Trial!

You have been provided with the raw `student_performance.csv` dataset containing missing test scores, absent attendance values, missing cities, and unencoded categorical variables.

Your quest is to execute the complete classroom data cleaning pipeline:

1. READ raw data
2. INSPECT missingness with `isna().sum()`
3. IMPUTE numeric columns (`Marks`, `Attendance`) using their medians
4. IMPUTE categorical columns (`City`, `Gender`) with `'Unknown'`
5. ENCODE categorical columns (`Gender`) using `pd.get_dummies(..., drop_first=True)`
6. EXPORT the pristine result to `cleaned_student_performance.csv` with `index=False`!

# df.to_csv("cleaned_student_performance.csv", index=False)
lessons.outputExample: Cleaned dataset saved with 0 missing values and dummy encoding.
lessons.tip: Execute each step with precision to purify the dataset.

challenges.title: Stage 1: Verify the Cleaning Sequence
challenges.instructions: According to the course notes, what is the correct sequence of the standard data cleaning pipeline?
challenges.question: What is the recommended data cleaning workflow?
options: A. READ -> INSPECT -> HANDLE MISSING VALUES -> ENCODE CATEGORIES -> VISUALIZE -> SAVE CLEANED DATA
B. SAVE CLEANED DATA -> DELETE RAW -> ENCODE -> READ
C. PLOT -> DROP EVERYTHING -> READ -> EXCEL
D. ENCODE CATEGORIES -> EXPORT -> READ -> INSPECT
challenges.answer: A. READ -> INSPECT -> HANDLE MISSING VALUES -> ENCODE CATEGORIES -> VISUALIZE -> SAVE CLEANED DATA
hints: Always inspect and clean before encoding and saving.
challenges.explanation: Correct! That is the official end-to-end data cleaning workflow from the classroom notes.

challenges.title: Stage 2: Impute Missing Numeric & Categorical
challenges.instructions: Execute numeric median imputation on 'Marks' and 'Attendance', and categorical imputation ('Unknown') on 'City' and 'Gender'. Print the total missing values across the DataFrame.
challenges.starterCode:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")

# 1. Impute numeric with median
df["Marks"] = df["Marks"].fillna(df["Marks"].median())
df["Attendance"] = df["Attendance"].fillna(df["Attendance"].median())

# 2. Impute categorical with 'Unknown'
df["City"] = df["City"].fillna("Unknown")
df["Gender"] = df["Gender"].fillna("Unknown")

print("Total missing values:", df.isna().sum().sum())
challenges.solution:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")
df["Marks"] = df["Marks"].fillna(df["Marks"].median())
df["Attendance"] = df["Attendance"].fillna(df["Attendance"].median())
df["City"] = df["City"].fillna("Unknown")
df["Gender"] = df["Gender"].fillna("Unknown")
print("Total missing values:", df.isna().sum().sum())
hints: Use .fillna(df['Marks'].median()) for Marks
Use .fillna('Unknown') for City and Gender
challenges.explanation: Outstanding! You eradicated all missing values across both numerical and categorical attributes.

challenges.title: Stage 3: Full End-to-End Purification & Export
challenges.instructions: Complete the full end-to-end pipeline: load data, impute Marks (median), impute Gender ('Unknown'), encode Gender with pd.get_dummies(..., drop_first=True, dtype=int), and save to 'cleaned_student_performance.csv' with index=False.
challenges.starterCode:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")

# Impute
df["Marks"] = df["Marks"].fillna(df["Marks"].median())
df["Gender"] = df["Gender"].fillna("Unknown")

# Encode Gender avoiding dummy trap
df = pd.get_dummies(df, columns=["Gender"], drop_first=True, dtype=int)

# Export cleaned dataset
df.to_csv("cleaned_student_performance.csv", index=False)
print("CLEAN DATA TRIAL MASTERED")
challenges.solution:
import pandas as pd
df = pd.read_csv("student_performance.csv")
df["Marks"] = df["Marks"].fillna(df["Marks"].median())
df["Gender"] = df["Gender"].fillna("Unknown")
df = pd.get_dummies(df, columns=["Gender"], drop_first=True, dtype=int)
df.to_csv("cleaned_student_performance.csv", index=False)
print("CLEAN DATA TRIAL MASTERED")
